title: GIGAWATT — the domain map
subtitle: From grid connection to useful compute. Follow the power, close the heat path, operate the system.
status: Planning baseline; expanded lessons, visuals and assessments are not yet implemented or reviewed.
scope: Modern AI data-center infrastructure, including conventional facilities and retrofit alternatives needed to explain engineering choices. System understanding and bounded quantitative decisions, not professional design qualification.
target_audience: Technically curious learners with arithmetic, percentages, unit conversion, simple graph reading and general computer literacy. No prior data-center, electrical, cooling or networking vocabulary is assumed. Explain additional algebra before relying on it; introduce specialized mathematics and professional practice only to the depth needed for the stated outcomes.
runtime: A substantial single course, potentially up to ten hours. Runtime is unallocated until section prototypes and learner rehearsals establish the depth each objective needs; this map is not a ten-hour script.

coverage_definition.partial: The current player teaches a useful fragment of this objective. It still needs expansion, an application assessment and review.
coverage_definition.missing: The current player does not substantively teach this objective. Related mentions or source links do not count as teaching.
coverage_definition.complete: Reserved for a scripted, implemented and reviewed objective with an application assessment. No objective is marked complete in this planning baseline.

evidence_policy: Source mappings identify research leads for domains, not verified support for every proposed claim or objective. The seed corpus is not exhaustive. Verify particular claims at lesson authoring, follow original references, retain dates and assumptions, and record contradictions rather than averaging them away.

lanes.title: Frame the system
lanes.description: Define quantities and the useful work the system must deliver.

lanes.title: Bring power to the racks
lanes.description: Connect, distribute, protect and convert electricity.

lanes.title: Turn hardware into useful work
lanes.description: Coordinate compute, memory, networks, storage and jobs.

lanes.title: Return the heat
lanes.description: Capture heat at the devices and reject it under real site conditions.

lanes.title: Build, operate and decide
lanes.description: Make the physical system deliverable, testable, maintainable and economically coherent.

domains.title: System boundaries and quantities
domains.question: What exactly does a megawatt of data-center capacity describe?
domains.purpose: Give every later calculation a unit, a boundary, and an operating condition.
scope: Campus, building, hall, row, rack, server, package and die
Power, energy, real/apparent power, efficiency and time
Nameplate, reserved, commissioned, available, demanded and productive capacity
Physical flows versus commercial relationships; reference designs versus actual sites

objectives.capability: Trace electrical energy, heat, and information through a data center while keeping the accounting boundaries separate.
objectives.assessment: Annotate one campus diagram with three paths and explain why useful computation and dissipated heat are not competing energy allocations.

objectives.capability: Convert power and energy across units and time; distinguish a measured load from a capacity rating.
objectives.assessment: Calculate an energy total from a stepped load profile and identify what cannot be inferred from a service rating.

objectives.capability: Define denominators for facility, IT and compute-only metrics and label the time window.
objectives.assessment: Reconcile a facility energy ledger with IT energy, overhead and a separately measured workload output.

objectives.capability: Separate physical principles, design specifications, observed deployments, announcements, forecasts and teaching assumptions.
objectives.assessment: Classify six supplied claims and state the additional evidence needed to call capacity operational.

visual.title: One campus, three paths
visual.interaction: Select power, heat or information, then zoom campus → rack → chip while retaining the enclosing boundary.
visual.prediction: Which quantities change when the accounting boundary moves from the utility meter to IT equipment?
visual.boundary: Arrows show connectivity and direction. Their animation does not represent physical propagation speed.

domains.worked_example: Use a synthetic 24-hour load trace to compare MW, MWh and separately specified capacity; label all measurement points.
domains.tradeoff: A simple system model is easier to reason with; omitted loads and changing boundaries can invalidate its conclusion.
domains.failure: A capacity headline combines planned expansion with an existing phase. Identify the double count before doing arithmetic.

domains.title: Workloads and the infrastructure brief
domains.question: What useful work must the facility deliver, and on what schedule?
domains.purpose: Derive infrastructure requirements from the service or job rather than starting with an equipment inventory.
scope: Training, inference and conventional services as different load and service profiles
Throughput, latency, availability, memory demand and utilization
Parallelism, communication, checkpointing and workload-driven power variation
Design envelopes and uncertainty; avoiding universal watts-to-tokens conversions

objectives.capability: Translate a workload brief into compute, memory, network, storage, power and service requirements.
objectives.assessment: Compare two supplied training and inference briefs and explain which requirements need measurement rather than a rack-count estimate.

objectives.capability: Distinguish hardware occupancy, power draw and productive utilization.
objectives.assessment: Explain three traces in which the same installed hardware produces different useful output; identify idle and waiting intervals.

objectives.capability: Explain how batching, parallel execution and synchronized job phases change the infrastructure demand profile.
objectives.assessment: Read a supplied job timeline and predict communication, checkpoint and load-transition intervals without assuming a universal waveform.

objectives.capability: State an infrastructure design envelope and identify which assumptions a benchmark can and cannot validate.
objectives.assessment: Write acceptance criteria for a hypothetical cluster using declared workload, precision, batch, latency and availability conditions.

visual.title: From job timeline to demand
visual.interaction: Switch between labeled training, interactive inference and batch inference scenarios; align work, communication and power traces.
visual.prediction: Does a higher average GPU power draw necessarily imply higher useful throughput?
visual.boundary: Traces are illustrative until tied to an identified measurement, workload and hardware configuration.

domains.worked_example: Compare a compute-limited and communication-limited synthetic job at identical installed power capacity; calculate elapsed time and useful work per energy.
domains.tradeoff: Provisioning for peaks, pooling resources and accepting queueing produce different cost and service outcomes.
domains.failure: A new workload meets the average MW budget but violates a latency or transient requirement.

domains.title: Siting, grid connection and supply
domains.question: Where can the required power actually arrive, and when?
domains.purpose: Connect the physical site decision to grid constraints, available infrastructure and the project schedule.
scope: Load connection, utility studies, substations, transmission and distribution interfaces
Generation and behind-the-meter supply where they affect delivery, dispatch or resilience
Capacity, energy, fuel, emissions, curtailment and time matching
Land, fiber, water, climate and local constraints as joint siting inputs

objectives.capability: Trace a physical supply path and distinguish it from a power purchase agreement or energy attribute claim.
objectives.assessment: Draw the metered connection separately from two commercial arrangements; name what each establishes.

objectives.capability: Explain voltage, current and conductor loss in a bounded AC or DC comparison.
objectives.assessment: Compare two balanced three-phase transfer scenarios with stated power factor and conductor resistance; list excluded losses.

objectives.capability: Explain the milestones and constraints between a proposed large load and service available to that load.
objectives.assessment: Turn a supplied project timeline into a capacity ledger without treating an application, agreement or energized substation as commissioned IT.

objectives.capability: Compare utility-only and on-site supply options against energy, capacity, fuel, grid and operating requirements.
objectives.assessment: Evaluate a synthetic siting brief with outage, fuel-delivery and curtailment constraints; record unresolved utility and local requirements.

visual.title: Two maps: electrons and agreements
visual.interaction: Overlay the physical connection, commercial contracts and project milestones on the same site comparison.
visual.prediction: Which contractual change increases physically deliverable power at the meter?
visual.boundary: A contract is not an electrical edge. Grid rules, interconnection terms and permits require a named jurisdiction and date.

domains.worked_example: Compare two hypothetical sites with different delivery dates, service limits, climate and fiber reach; keep ratings, costs and operating assumptions explicit.
domains.tradeoff: Earlier on-site supply may trade schedule advantage against fuel, emissions, operating complexity and future grid integration.
domains.failure: Supply is available in aggregate but a transmission constraint or fuel interruption prevents the promised operating profile.

domains.title: Campus and building power distribution
domains.question: How does power get from the connection to each load?
domains.purpose: Teach electrical topology, equipment roles and rating boundaries before comparing architecture changes.
scope: Single-line diagrams and voltage levels
Transformers, switchgear, switchboards, busway, cables and distribution units
Real/apparent power, power factor, efficiency, harmonic and thermal limits
AC distribution and alternative DC conversion locations
House loads, IT loads, reserved capacity and expansion phases

objectives.capability: Read a generic single-line diagram and explain what each distribution component changes, measures, switches or protects.
objectives.assessment: Annotate an unfamiliar generic diagram and identify the loads behind each boundary.

objectives.capability: Translate load requirements into currents and equipment loading without confusing kW with kVA or nameplate with usable capacity.
objectives.assessment: Calculate loading in a stated balanced scenario, including conversion efficiency and a supplied power factor; explain missing design inputs.

objectives.capability: Compare centralized and distributed conversion and identify which conductors, equipment and loss boundaries change.
objectives.assessment: Mark the changed interfaces on AC, near-rack DC and facility DC reference diagrams without claiming one universal efficiency improvement.

objectives.capability: Reconcile IT and auxiliary loads with a downstream electrical capacity budget across project phases.
objectives.assessment: Find the binding transformer, feeder or service constraint in a synthetic phase-opening plan.

visual.title: A living single-line diagram
visual.interaction: Select a load to trace its upstream path; switch between conversion placements and display currents at labeled boundaries.
visual.prediction: Which current changes when conversion moves upstream, and which upstream current may remain essentially unchanged?
visual.boundary: A teaching topology is not an as-built design, a protection study or a conductor sizing tool.

domains.worked_example: Work through one assumed facility-to-rack power budget, including conversion losses and separately reserved auxiliary loads.
domains.tradeoff: Centralization can change conversion count, serviceability and fault scope; actual benefits depend on the selected topology and operating point.
domains.failure: A row can fit physically while exceeding a feeder's available rating after required reserves.

domains.title: Continuity, storage and protection
domains.question: What survives a disturbance, and for how long?
domains.purpose: Connect backup supply, fault isolation and maintenance to complete operating paths.
scope: UPS, batteries, generators, transfer sequences and load shedding
Stored energy versus discharge power; transient response versus outage duration
N, N+1, 2N, common-mode failures and maintainability
Grounding, fault detection, selective isolation and AC/DC protection concepts
Electrical and thermal ride-through together

objectives.capability: Calculate bounded stored-energy runtime while checking discharge power and reserve assumptions.
objectives.assessment: Compare two storage systems with the same MWh but different MW limits; explain why neither energy alone nor nameplate guarantees ride-through.

objectives.capability: Trace an interruption, transfer and restoration sequence including IT, cooling and controls.
objectives.assessment: Predict which loads remain supported at each step of a supplied sequence; identify a missing auxiliary supply.

objectives.capability: Evaluate path independence and surviving capacity during both a fault and planned maintenance.
objectives.assessment: Find a common-mode dependency in a two-feed diagram and calculate load support with one path unavailable.

objectives.capability: Explain why fault clearing and grounding require topology-specific AC/DC protection design.
objectives.assessment: Compare two conceptual isolation sequences and list the protection evidence needed before endorsing either architecture.

visual.title: Failure timeline and surviving paths
visual.interaction: Inject an outage or isolate equipment; run a discrete sequence with separate electrical, thermal and control availability tracks.
visual.prediction: Can the rack remain energized while the overall service still becomes unavailable?
visual.boundary: Timing and reliability values are declared scenarios, not device guarantees or a Tier certification.

domains.worked_example: Calculate a storage energy budget and a surviving-path power budget separately, then test whether both support the same required interval.
domains.tradeoff: More redundant equipment may improve maintainability but can add shared controls, switching complexity and underutilized capacity.
domains.failure: A successful electrical transfer leaves cooling controls unavailable; determine the missing evidence for thermal ride-through.

domains.title: Rack power and the 800 V DC transition
domains.question: Where should voltage conversion happen as rack demand changes?
domains.purpose: Use 800 V DC as an architecture comparison grounded in current, interfaces and deployment constraints.
scope: Power shelves, rack buses, converters, point-of-load regulation and auxiliary loads
Conventional AC-to-rack conversion, sidecars and broader facility DC options
800 V DC and other specified voltage arrangements; product/version boundaries
Copper, connectors, busbars, stored energy, service access and space
Load transients, protection interfaces, brownfield and greenfield choices

objectives.capability: Trace conversion from rack input to processor rails and distinguish whole-rack power from chip power.
objectives.assessment: Label every voltage and power boundary on two supplied rack diagrams and reject a misleading per-GPU TDP calculation.

objectives.capability: Quantify how distribution voltage changes current at fixed DC power without treating conductor loss as total system efficiency.
objectives.assessment: Compute currents for a declared 100 kW DC boundary at 50 V and 800 V, then state why this does not size a real conductor or establish an efficiency delta.

objectives.capability: Compare near-rack sidecars, rack-level conversion and facility DC as distinct architectures.
objectives.assessment: Place conversion, storage, protection and AC/DC boundaries for each; distinguish announced products from proposed future designs.

objectives.capability: Evaluate a rack power upgrade against connector, bus, protection, auxiliary and transient interfaces.
objectives.assessment: Write an interface checklist for a synthetic higher-density rack migration, with every unknown left explicit.

objectives.capability: Explain how retrofit constraints can reverse a seemingly attractive greenfield architecture choice.
objectives.assessment: Choose between two supplied migration paths using space, downtime, conversion and maintenance assumptions; show what would change the decision.

visual.title: Move the conversion boundary
visual.interaction: Morph a shared diagram between existing AC, sidecar and broader DC reference architectures; keep unchanged equipment visually anchored.
visual.prediction: Which constraints move, which remain, and where does a new protection or service interface appear?
visual.boundary: Use dated, identified reference architectures. Single-ended and bipolar voltage labels cannot be silently interchanged; benefits require stated comparisons.

domains.worked_example: At a hypothetical 100 kW DC boundary, compare 50 V and 800 V currents; separately account for each assumed conversion stage and its load-dependent efficiency.
domains.tradeoff: Higher distribution voltage changes current and packaging constraints while introducing different conversion, insulation, protection and service requirements.
domains.failure: A proposed sidecar upgrade clears rack space but does not solve an upstream AC feeder limit.

domains.title: Compute, memory and the rack
domains.question: What inside the rack determines useful performance?
domains.purpose: Explain hardware organization only as deeply as needed to connect workload progress with infrastructure choices.
scope: CPU, accelerator, memory, host and accelerator interconnect roles
Memory capacity and bandwidth, compute throughput and data movement
Server, tray, rack and scale-up system boundaries
Packaging and power/thermal density where they affect the facility
Product specifications, measured performance and workload-dependent limits

objectives.capability: Locate compute, memory and communication components within a server and rack and explain their roles.
objectives.assessment: Trace a simplified data path from storage through host memory to accelerator memory and compute.

objectives.capability: Distinguish memory-capacity, memory-bandwidth, compute and communication limits.
objectives.assessment: Use supplied workload and hardware numbers to identify a plausible bottleneck and state the model's assumptions.

objectives.capability: Explain why chip count, advertised FLOPS and installed MW cannot independently establish job throughput.
objectives.assessment: Compare two synthetic rack configurations with equal power envelopes but different memory and communication constraints.

objectives.capability: Connect server and rack organization to power, cooling, weight and maintenance interfaces.
objectives.assessment: Identify the facility interface changes caused by replacing an air-cooled server row with a specified dense rack-scale system.

visual.title: A rack as a data path
visual.interaction: Zoom rack → tray → package; highlight storage transfers, memory access, compute and scale-up communication with consistent boundaries.
visual.prediction: Which upgrade helps a workload that is waiting on memory rather than arithmetic?
visual.boundary: Use product-specific diagrams only with versions and sources. The generic data path is deliberately simplified.

domains.worked_example: Apply a supplied compute/bandwidth model to two workloads, then explain which unmodeled communication or software effects could reduce throughput.
domains.tradeoff: More tightly integrated systems can change performance and data movement while constraining service granularity and upgrade choices.
domains.failure: A failed component changes the usable topology and job capacity even though facility electrical capacity is unchanged.

domains.title: Networking and interconnects
domains.question: How do many devices make progress as one system?
domains.purpose: Teach communication cost and topology as constraints on useful compute and physical deployment.
scope: Scale-up, scale-out and inter-data-center networking
Latency, bandwidth, bisection capacity, oversubscription and congestion
Collectives, routing and workload placement
Ethernet and InfiniBand as architectures with implementation-specific behavior
Copper, pluggable optics and co-packaged optics; reach, power, cabling and serviceability

objectives.capability: Distinguish scale-up, scale-out and wide-area communication requirements.
objectives.assessment: Place three communication patterns on a rack, cluster and regional map and identify the relevant bottleneck.

objectives.capability: Calculate an illustrative topology's endpoint ports, oversubscription and transfer-time lower bounds.
objectives.assessment: Compare two small supplied topologies, including units and stated routing assumptions; identify why bandwidth alone does not predict application time.

objectives.capability: Explain how congestion, collectives and topology-aware placement affect job progress.
objectives.assessment: Predict the effect of a constrained link during a collective and describe a placement or architecture alternative.

objectives.capability: Compare interconnect media and packaging choices using reach, bandwidth, power, cooling and replacement boundaries.
objectives.assessment: Evaluate copper, pluggable optics and a specified CPO proposal for a declared use case without treating a roadmap as a deployed default.

objectives.capability: Trace a network failure or degraded link into workload, cabling and operational consequences.
objectives.assessment: Explain why a powered and cooled cluster can miss its useful-throughput acceptance target after a partial fabric failure.

visual.title: Watch a collective cross the fabric
visual.interaction: Advance a small collective step by step; change topology, oversubscription or a failed link and compare work/wait timelines.
visual.prediction: Does doubling a single link's bandwidth halve the whole job time?
visual.boundary: A simplified communication model is not a benchmark. Keep routing, concurrency, protocol overhead and failure assumptions visible.

domains.worked_example: Calculate ports and idealized transfer bounds for a small fabric, then add explicitly modeled communication phases to a job timeline.
domains.tradeoff: Bandwidth density, reach, power and serviceability pull in different directions; network selection depends on workload and operating capability.
domains.failure: A partial fabric degradation increases job waiting while aggregate device health appears normal.

domains.title: Storage, orchestration and recovery
domains.question: Can data and jobs reach the hardware, and can useful progress survive failures?
domains.purpose: Connect storage and cluster software to the delivery of a usable service.
scope: Local, shared and object storage roles; bandwidth, latency, metadata and durability
Dataset ingestion, checkpointing and restart paths
Scheduling, topology-aware placement and resource isolation
Cluster bring-up, provisioning, observability and tenant/service acceptance
Recovery objectives, redundancy and backup as different concepts

objectives.capability: Trace the dataset and checkpoint paths and distinguish capacity, throughput and metadata constraints.
objectives.assessment: Calculate an idealized checkpoint transfer time from supplied sizes and effective bandwidth, then identify additional bottlenecks.

objectives.capability: Explain how checkpoint frequency, failure behavior and restart time affect completed work.
objectives.assessment: Compare two explicit checkpoint policies on a synthetic timeline that includes a failure and recovery.

objectives.capability: Explain scheduling, placement, provisioning and isolation as prerequisites for usable cluster capacity.
objectives.assessment: Diagnose a scenario in which hardware is healthy but jobs cannot obtain the required topology, software environment or storage access.

objectives.capability: Specify a service acceptance exercise that tests end-to-end data access, job launch, useful output and recovery.
objectives.assessment: Write a reproducible test plan for a synthetic tenant without reducing acceptance to a device-count or power-on check.

visual.title: Progress survives—or starts again
visual.interaction: Run the same job with two checkpoint/restart policies; show useful work, storage traffic, saved state and lost progress.
visual.prediction: Can a faster checkpoint policy consume enough resources to slow normal progress?
visual.boundary: Do not assume independent failures or constant restart time without labeling them; RAID/replication and backup are distinct.

domains.worked_example: Reconcile checkpoint size, sustained storage throughput and recovery time for a provided scenario; account separately for lost and recomputed work.
domains.tradeoff: More frequent checkpoints can reduce lost progress but consume storage, network and execution resources.
domains.failure: A storage or orchestration failure makes otherwise available GPUs unusable or prevents a clean restart.

domains.title: Chip and rack heat capture
domains.question: How does heat leave the devices without exceeding their operating limits?
domains.purpose: Connect local thermal constraints with airflow, coolant and rack interfaces.
scope: Heat generation, heat flux, thermal resistance and temperature limits
Heat sinks, cold plates, rear-door exchangers, immersion and two-phase alternatives
Residual air paths and containment
Technology coolant, manifolds, quick disconnects and CDUs
Flow, pressure drop, approach temperature, material compatibility and leak management

objectives.capability: Trace parallel air and liquid heat paths and explain why rack power alone does not specify local cooling difficulty.
objectives.assessment: Compare two hypothetical devices with the same total heat but different heat flux or thermal resistance.

objectives.capability: Calculate a single-phase heat-transport flow under stated fluid and temperature assumptions.
objectives.assessment: Solve a heat/flow/temperature-rise example and explain why the result alone does not select a pump or cold plate.

objectives.capability: Explain a CDU's fluid separation, heat-exchange and control functions while distinguishing loop rise from approach temperature.
objectives.assessment: Draw two closed loops, label their temperature points and predict the effect of a constrained heat-exchanger interface.

objectives.capability: Compare air, cold-plate, rear-door and immersion approaches against a declared density and service brief.
objectives.assessment: Evaluate a synthetic retrofit with residual-air, fluid, pressure, access and maintenance requirements; identify missing compatibility evidence.

visual.title: Two fluids, one heat transfer
visual.interaction: Follow heat from die through parallel air/liquid routes; vary flow and supply temperature within a declared model.
visual.prediction: Does increasing loop temperature rise imply the same change in heat-exchanger approach temperature?
visual.boundary: Fluid properties and operating limits must be specified. Flow arithmetic is not a hydraulic or equipment selection model.

domains.worked_example: Calculate water flow for a declared steady heat load, then examine a supplied pressure-drop curve and a separate heat-exchanger approach constraint.
domains.tradeoff: Capturing heat closer to its source can support density while changing plumbing, materials, controls and service procedures.
domains.failure: A blocked branch or failed pump creates a local thermal limit that a facility-wide MW heat balance cannot reveal.

domains.title: Heat rejection, climate and water
domains.question: Where does the heat finally go, and what does moving it consume?
domains.purpose: Close the energy and water balances through facility cooling and the outdoor environment.
scope: Facility water loops, pumps, air handlers and thermal storage
Dry coolers, chillers, towers and economizers as distinct systems
Refrigeration, COP, load dependence and added compressor heat
Dry-bulb/wet-bulb conditions, water supply, treatment and consumption
PUE/WUE boundaries, heat reuse and environmental tradeoffs

objectives.capability: Distinguish dry cooling, refrigeration, evaporative rejection and economizer operating modes.
objectives.assessment: Trace four reference heat paths and identify where electricity and water enter each.

objectives.capability: Close a declared chiller energy balance and calculate cooling COP with the correct numerator and denominator.
objectives.assessment: Given cooling duty and compressor input, calculate COP and condenser heat; place pumps and fans at their stated boundaries.

objectives.capability: Explain how ambient conditions, supply temperatures and equipment performance constrain capacity and economizer operation.
objectives.assessment: Use supplied equipment curves and weather bins to compare two operating modes without applying a universal free-cooling threshold.

objectives.capability: Compute energy and water metrics with explicit boundaries and distinguish consumption from withdrawal.
objectives.assessment: Compare two scenarios over the same period using stated facility/IT energies and water accounting; explain what PUE and WUE omit.

objectives.capability: Evaluate cooling architecture or heat reuse against climate, water, electrical capacity and receiving-load constraints.
objectives.assessment: Compare a hot-weather and a water-constrained site using a supplied design brief; identify what changes the preferred choice.

visual.title: The heat balance meets the weather
visual.interaction: Sweep a labeled ambient condition through supplied performance curves; watch available cooling, plant power and water use together.
visual.prediction: Under a fixed site electrical limit, can hotter weather constrain IT twice: through cooling capacity and auxiliary demand?
visual.boundary: COP and equipment curves need rating conditions. Water use depends on system and accounting boundary, not the label liquid cooling.

domains.worked_example: Use a synthetic chiller performance table and hourly weather bins to estimate cooling electricity; keep the separate water model's assumptions explicit.
domains.tradeoff: Temperature, water, energy, space and heat-reuse opportunities create site-specific choices rather than a universal best cooling system.
domains.failure: A heatwave or water restriction invalidates a nominal cooling rating used in the electrical capacity plan.

domains.title: Physical site, buildings and safety
domains.question: What must the actual place support beyond electrical and thermal ratings?
domains.purpose: Make spatial, environmental, access and safety constraints visible before treating a schematic as buildable.
scope: Land, geotechnical and civil interfaces; buildings, structural loading and floor layouts
Flood, seismic, weather and other site hazards as jurisdiction-specific inputs
Equipment access, lifting, replacement routes, egress and service clearances
Fire detection/suppression, electrical hazards and battery/fuel arrangements at conceptual level
Physical security and OT/IT trust boundaries; noise, water and environmental permits

objectives.capability: Translate a reference equipment layout into space, weight, access and replacement-route requirements.
objectives.assessment: Reject a synthetic rack/plant layout that fits in area but fails a supplied loading or service-access constraint.

objectives.capability: Identify site hazards and permitting interfaces that require location-specific evidence.
objectives.assessment: Build a siting risk register for two hypothetical locations and distinguish generic questions from verified local requirements.

objectives.capability: Explain how fire, electrical, fluid and stored-energy hazards influence layout and operating boundaries.
objectives.assessment: Annotate a conceptual layout with required specialist reviews and separation/access questions without presenting it as a compliant design.

objectives.capability: Trace physical and control-system access boundaries and explain why availability depends on controlled changes and access.
objectives.assessment: Identify a shared access or control dependency in a supplied facility/tenant interface diagram.

visual.title: The schematic has to fit somewhere
visual.interaction: Switch a hall between normal operation, equipment replacement and emergency-access views; reveal footprints and clearance envelopes.
visual.prediction: Can a higher-density rack reduce rack count while making the existing building harder to use?
visual.boundary: Illustrative envelopes are not code-compliant dimensions. Applicable requirements depend on jurisdiction, equipment and design review.

domains.worked_example: Fit a hypothetical rack and replacement route into a supplied floor plan using declared dimensions and structural limits.
domains.tradeoff: Density and compactness must be weighed against access, hazard separation, replacement logistics and expansion space.
domains.failure: A component cannot be replaced while maintaining the planned service path, despite adequate spare electrical capacity.

domains.title: Design, procurement and commissioning
domains.question: How does a design become a tested, usable service?
domains.purpose: Teach delivery as a chain of interfaces and evidence, not a chronology of announcements.
scope: Requirements, design basis, interface ownership and change control
Equipment lead times, factory testing, logistics and sequencing
Construction, installation quality, fluid cleanliness and pre-functional checks
Functional and integrated systems testing, failure scenarios and acceptance
Phased handover, as-built records, procedures and operator training

objectives.capability: Build a dependency-based delivery plan and distinguish a critical path from the longest equipment lead time.
objectives.assessment: Sequence a synthetic project with parallel procurement, utility work, installation and testing; identify which delay changes service availability.

objectives.capability: Track interface requirements across vendors and design changes.
objectives.assessment: Diagnose a rack/CDU or power/control interface mismatch before equipment shipment and state the acceptance evidence required.

objectives.capability: Distinguish installed, energized, individually tested, integrated-tested and service-accepted states.
objectives.assessment: Classify supplied milestone evidence and identify which complete electrical, thermal and information paths remain unproven.

objectives.capability: Specify an integrated acceptance and handover plan for a phased deployment.
objectives.assessment: Propose normal, failure, maintenance and recovery tests, instrumentation, acceptance criteria, records and operator handover for a synthetic phase.

visual.title: Only complete paths count
visual.interaction: Advance independent delivery milestones across power, cooling, network and controls; reveal when a complete tested service path exists.
visual.prediction: Can the utility milestone be complete while the usable-capacity milestone remains unchanged?
visual.boundary: Testing requirements and acceptance conditions must be tied to a project brief. Timeline bars do not prove operating status.

domains.worked_example: Find the earliest service-ready date in a supplied dependency graph, then recalculate after a converter or cooling-control delivery delay.
domains.tradeoff: Standardization and early ordering can accelerate delivery while limiting later changes; phased openings add interface and acceptance complexity.
domains.failure: Individually successful subsystem tests miss a coupled failure during an integrated utility-loss test.

domains.title: Controls, operations and reliability
domains.question: How does the system remain within its limits after handover?
domains.purpose: Turn the static design into monitored operation, maintenance and incident recovery.
scope: Electrical, building, cooling and cluster monitoring; meters, sensors and control loops
Setpoints, sequences, alarms, telemetry quality and control dependencies
Maintenance, procedures, staffing, change/configuration management and spares
Failure domains, common causes, service availability and incident learning
Workload load changes, capacity management, aging and retrofit operations

objectives.capability: Place sensors and meters so an operator can distinguish an actual constraint from missing or misleading telemetry.
objectives.assessment: Diagnose a synthetic thermal alarm using a labeled trend set; state where additional measurements are needed.

objectives.capability: Explain the difference between a device controller, a facility sequence and workload scheduling.
objectives.assessment: Trace a supplied setpoint or load change through these layers and identify the required coordination and limits.

objectives.capability: Evaluate maintainability using a procedure, surviving capacity and real isolation boundaries.
objectives.assessment: Walk through a synthetic maintenance plan and identify the shared dependency or restoration step that threatens service.

objectives.capability: Distinguish component reliability, topology claims and measured service availability.
objectives.assessment: Critique a naive multiplication of component availabilities and specify which correlated failures and repair assumptions are missing.

objectives.capability: Convert a failure or capacity incident into an evidence-based recovery and prevention plan.
objectives.assessment: Reconstruct a supplied incident timeline, separate observations from hypotheses, and propose a verification step for each corrective action.

visual.title: Operate the same campus
visual.interaction: Move from topology to aligned telemetry and an incident timeline; select a maintenance action or workload change and trace dependencies.
visual.prediction: Which alarm is a symptom, and what observation would discriminate between two plausible causes?
visual.boundary: Synthetic telemetry is labeled. A simplified control model cannot establish stability, safety or field performance.

domains.worked_example: Use a synthetic availability and incident log to calculate service downtime and identify the difference between equipment uptime and completed work.
domains.tradeoff: Aggressive utilization or efficiency setpoints may reduce margin; the operational choice depends on measured behavior and service requirements.
domains.failure: A shared control or configuration change disables nominally independent equipment paths.

domains.title: Capacity, cost and system decisions
domains.question: Which constraint limits useful service, and which change is worth making?
domains.purpose: Combine engineering, delivery and workload models into a bounded decision with explicit uncertainty.
scope: Capacity ledgers, bottlenecks, reserves and phased expansion
Capital and operating costs, ownership/lease boundaries and commercial commitments
Energy, hardware utilization, financing assumptions and time to service
Cost per useful workload outcome versus cost per MW or GPU-hour
Sensitivity, scenarios, uncertainty, retrofit and retirement

objectives.capability: Reconcile electrical, thermal, spatial, network and commissioned-service limits using the same boundaries.
objectives.assessment: Calculate a synthetic capacity ceiling and identify tied constraints without treating it as measured operating demand.

objectives.capability: Build an auditable cost model that separates capital, energy, operations, ownership and financing assumptions.
objectives.assessment: Compare two supplied ownership or service models over an explicit horizon with a consistent denominator and utilization scenario.

objectives.capability: Explain why cost per MW, per installed accelerator and per useful result answer different questions.
objectives.assessment: Recalculate a scenario after changing throughput or utilization while leaving installed capacity constant.

objectives.capability: Evaluate an upgrade using sensitivity to delivery date, service output, efficiency and constraints.
objectives.assessment: Choose a synthetic power, cooling or network investment and identify the assumptions that reverse its ranking.

objectives.capability: Audit a named project's public evidence without filling unknown capacity, topology or economics with generic assumptions.
objectives.assessment: Produce a dated case ledger separating announced, designed, permitted, commissioned and observed facts; list unresolved questions.

visual.title: Find the constraint, then change it
visual.interaction: Compare a base case and one intervention across capacity, time, cost and useful output; display assumptions beside the result.
visual.prediction: Does removing the current bottleneck necessarily increase delivered useful work or improve cost per result?
visual.boundary: A scenario is not a valuation, site estimate or throughput forecast. Do not add overlapping capacity stages or count shared loads twice.

domains.worked_example: Extend the existing 100 MW teaching scenario with separate non-compute IT, commissioning, workload and delivery assumptions; compare two interventions.
domains.tradeoff: Lowest capital cost, earliest service, highest efficiency and best useful-output economics may select different designs.
domains.failure: A technically successful upgrade leaves a separate delivery, network or workload constraint binding.

paths.title: Power → rack
paths.purpose: Physical electrical journey. This is a conceptual path, not a universal installed topology.

paths.title: Chip → environment
paths.purpose: Thermal journey, including parallel air/liquid paths and auxiliary heat inputs.

paths.title: Workload → useful service
paths.purpose: Information and service dependencies, not a literal packet route.

paths.title: Site → service → upgrade
paths.purpose: A lifecycle view across domains. Design and procurement iterate; this is not a strict construction schedule.

sequence.title: See the system and define the job
sequence.outcome: Establish the vocabulary, three paths and the workload brief used throughout.

sequence.title: Find a site and deliver power
sequence.outcome: Make the physical location, utility connection and single-line diagram legible.

sequence.title: Keep it running and enter the rack
sequence.outcome: Compare continuity and conversion choices, including 800 V DC, against interfaces and failures.

sequence.title: Make the cluster productive
sequence.outcome: Connect compute, memory, communication, storage and scheduling to useful progress.

sequence.title: Close the heat and water balances
sequence.outcome: Follow heat from local device limits to climate-dependent rejection and resource use.

sequence.title: Deliver, operate and make decisions
sequence.outcome: Test complete service paths, operate them, and defend a system decision with uncertainty.

capstones.title: Grid interruption with a thermal dependency
capstones.brief: A utility interruption occurs in a hypothetical facility. IT storage support and cooling/control supply paths are specified separately.
capstones.deliverable: An annotated topology, discrete failure timeline, energy and power budgets, and a list of missing thermal evidence.
capstones.assessment: Find the unsupported auxiliary path; distinguish what is electrically sustained from what can continue delivering service. Do not invent a thermal ride-through time.

capstones.title: Hot weather under a fixed site power limit
capstones.brief: Ambient conditions move across supplied cooling performance curves while the site electrical limit remains fixed.
capstones.deliverable: A before/after power and heat balance with binding constraints and a stated operating response.
capstones.assessment: Account for changed cooling capacity and auxiliary draw separately; explain why an annual PUE is not an instantaneous plant model.

capstones.title: A denser rack in an existing building
capstones.brief: Compare a higher-density rack migration using the existing AC plant, a sidecar option and a separately specified broader DC alternative.
capstones.deliverable: Interface matrix, conversion diagrams, current and heat-flow calculations, floor/service-access review, migration sequence and scenario cost comparison.
capstones.assessment: Identify retained upstream constraints and new interfaces; separate reference specifications, roadmap claims and hypothetical assumptions.

capstones.title: A powered cluster that misses its job target
capstones.brief: The hardware has adequate power and cooling, but a synthetic workload suffers fabric congestion and checkpoint stalls.
capstones.deliverable: Work/wait/recovery timeline, a bounded bottleneck calculation, and an experiment that distinguishes competing causes.
capstones.assessment: Use evidence to distinguish a communication/storage constraint from a compute shortfall; do not infer output from MW.

capstones.title: Open one phase of a campus
capstones.brief: An illustrative project has utility service, some installed racks and uneven subsystem completion. A separate named-site exercise uses only dated public evidence.
capstones.deliverable: Capacity-state ledger, dependency schedule, integrated acceptance plan and unresolved-evidence list.
capstones.assessment: Count only complete, accepted service paths for the synthetic brief; leave the named site's unestablished commissioning and demand values unknown.

exclusions.topic: Full semiconductor manufacturing and transistor/device physics
exclusions.reason: CHIPS and specialist material own fabrication depth. Here packaging, devices and memory matter where they change rack and facility requirements.
exclusions.reentry: Include a mechanism when it is necessary to explain a compute, electrical or thermal interface.

exclusions.topic: Detailed electrical, structural, fire or mechanical design qualification
exclusions.reason: This course teaches interpretation and bounded reasoning, not stamped designs, field switching procedures or jurisdiction-wide compliance.
exclusions.reentry: Teach the relevant design question and point to dated local requirements and qualified review; do not omit safety interfaces.

exclusions.topic: A complete generation-technology or electricity-market survey
exclusions.reason: Depth is limited to the supply, fuel, interconnection, emissions and commercial distinctions needed for data-center decisions.
exclusions.reentry: Include a supply option when it materially changes deliverability, operating behavior or project economics.

exclusions.topic: Supplier rankings, investment recommendations and exhaustive company histories
exclusions.reason: The curriculum is organized around capabilities and decisions. Company detail is a dated example, not the organizing principle.
exclusions.reentry: Use a sourced case when it explains a specific architecture, delivery constraint or measurable tradeoff.

exclusions.topic: Full GPU programming, model training and cloud administration tutorials
exclusions.reason: Workload and software mechanisms are included to explain infrastructure behavior; implementing every software layer would be a separate course.
exclusions.reentry: Include a small reproducible experiment when it tests an infrastructure learning objective.

exclusions.reason: Modern AI facilities are the center. Conventional and retrofit configurations are taught where they establish prerequisites or meaningful alternatives.
exclusions.reentry: Include a contrasting case when it changes an assumption in the central model.

production_priorities: Prototype one electrical architecture comparison, one thermal model and one network/recovery scenario before allocating runtime.
Review prerequisites and first-use vocabulary against the six-act sequence; domain IDs are stable reference IDs, not chapter numbers.
Expand the seed source catalog into a dated article inventory; record access/review status, domain mappings, duplicates, exclusions and unresolved primary evidence.
At lesson authoring, map each objective to exact claims, citations, original visual assets and an application assessment. A domain-level source link is not sufficient.
Obtain separate electrical/facilities and cluster/network technical reviews, then rehearse dense sections with intended learners.
Publish the long-form recording with navigable text, source dates, glossary, calculators and an errata location; maintain the companion when implementations change.
anti_pattern: The encyclopedic survey: naming every component, paraphrasing every article, animating an inventory or increasing runtime without teaching a mechanism, worked example, consequential tradeoff, failure or limiting case, and transfer to a changed situation.
